sections.title: Reading the king’s position
paras: Every checkmate comes down to two facts: the king is in check, and it has no safe square. Recognizing mating patterns starts with counting a king’s escape squares.

Look at every square next to the enemy king. Some are blocked by its own pieces, some are covered by your pieces, and the rest are escape squares. When a king has none or one, a single check may be mate. When it has several, you need more force or a sacrifice to take them away.
Kings that have castled behind unmoved pawns often have no escape squares at all. That is a strength in the opening and a weakness later.
sections.key: Count the king’s escape squares before you look for checks. The fewer it has, the closer mate is.

sections.title: Back-rank mates
paras: When a king sits on its first rank behind its own pawns, those pawns take away its escape squares. A rook or queen that reaches the back rank with check can then give mate, unless a defender covers that rank in time.
The pattern appears constantly because defenders get pulled away. If the only piece guarding the back rank is attacked or overloaded, the mate becomes possible.
The cure is a single pawn move that gives the king a flight square, often called luft.
sections.key: Count the defenders of the back rank. If an attacker arrives there with check and nothing can block or capture, it is mate.

sections.title: Mates with the queen
paras: The queen covers more squares than any other piece, so most mates involve her. On her own she can mate a king on the edge of the board when her own king or another piece protects her.

The most common pattern is the queen landing right next to the enemy king, defended by another piece, so the king can neither capture her nor escape. A queen supported by a pawn or a bishop in front of a castled king is a classic example.
When you see a supported square next to the enemy king, check whether your queen can reach it.
sections.key: A defended queen next to the king, with every escape square covered, is mate.

sections.title: Mates with rooks
paras: Rooks give mate along ranks and files. Two rooks working together can drive a king to the edge by checking on alternate ranks, and a rook on the seventh or eighth rank combined with a minor piece or a pawn produces many standard mates.
A rook on an open file next to the enemy king, supported by another piece, is a recurring finish. So is a rook check on the edge when the king’s escape squares are covered by a knight or bishop.
Look for open files and ranks leading to the king, and for squares where a rook check can’t be blocked.
sections.key: A rook check along an open line, with the escape squares covered by another piece, is a common mating finish.

sections.title: Knight and bishop patterns
paras: Knights and bishops give some of the most striking mates. A knight can mate a king that is completely surrounded by its own pieces, the smothered mate, because nothing can block a knight check.
Two bishops on adjacent diagonals can trap a king in the open, and a knight working with a rook or bishop can cover exactly the squares the king needs.
These patterns are easy to miss because the minor pieces look harmless from a distance. Train your eye to see the squares they control next to the enemy king.
sections.key: When the king is hemmed in by its own pieces, a knight check may be mate, because a knight check can’t be blocked.

sections.title: Opening the king
paras: A well-protected king can still be mated if the protection is removed. Sacrifices that destroy the pawn cover, deflect a defender or drag the king into the open are the bridge between a strong attack and a mating pattern.
Before you sacrifice, picture the position after the sacrifice and ask which mating pattern you are heading for. If you can name the final pattern, the sacrifice is usually sound.
In the positions that follow, the first move gives up material and the mate comes a move later.
sections.key: Sacrifice with a destination: know which mating pattern the sacrifice leads to before you play it.
